input: "Mostly stories. I give imaginary people better lines than I ever manage for myself. Occasionally letters." I glance at my ink-stained fingers. "I'd like to see an instrument improved by being unreliable." Then I turn to Rashid. "You've accounted for Ashara's afternoon. What would you do with one that belonged entirely to you?"
output:
Ashara’s tail stills over the leg of her chair.

“I account for my own afternoons,” she says. Not sharply, exactly. Precisely.

Rashid inclines his head to her at once. “You do. I supplied corroboration, not ownership.”

Then your question catches him more cleanly than the teasing did. He looks down at the careful arrangement of his knife and fork, dark fur visible along the back of one hand.

“An afternoon entirely mine?” he repeats. “I would write my sister a proper letter. She is eleven and has begun accusing me of correspondence conducted under duress.” His mouth shifts, almost a smile. “She is not wrong. Then I would sleep until sunset.”

“Revolutionary,” Ashara says.

“Please don’t report me.”

Seraphel’s blue eyes brighten.

“At eleven, a sister plainly knows  
Which polished excuse is just for show.”

“That also is regrettably true,” Rashid says.

Caelindra’s ears have angled toward you at the mention of stories. She takes a measured bite of greens before saying, “Do these imaginary people of yours make poor decisions? Or do you rescue them with better lines before they can?”

Beside you, Ysolde sets down her spoon. “The western terrace has an anemometer the storm has confused.” Her voice is quiet enough that the table leans into it without meaning to. “It reports the wind several minutes before the wind arrives. The astronomers call it broken.”

“And you disagree,” you say.

“I find it more interesting than one which merely works.”

The corner of her mouth moves—not quite a smile, but near enough to count.

“I am going after dinner,” she says. “You may see it, if curiosity survives the roast.”

A server uncovers the next platter. Herb-scented steam rises between the candles, and Caelindra gives you a cool, assessing look across it.

“Bring one of these stories, then,” she says. “A short one. I refuse to lose sleep discovering you are sentimental.”
